sources.title: Qiu Jin (Q465324), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-23): English label 'Qiu Jin', description 'Chinese revolutionary, feminist, and writer (1875-1907)', Korean label 추근, born 8 November 1875 (a second, lower-ranked value of 1879 is also stored), died July 1907 (15 or 17 July values stored), citizen of the Qing dynasty, instance of human. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Karen Gernant, 'Qiu Jin (c. 1875-1907)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale; read in full on Encyclopedia.com, including its bibliography of Chinese and Western scholarship). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Chinese revolutionary, poet and feminist executed in 1907 for her part in an attempted rising against the Qing; left her husband and two children in 1904 to study in Japan; joined the Revolutionary Alliance in 1905 and was named head of its Zhejiang branch; founded the Chinese Women's Journal in Shanghai (first issue 14 January 1907, only two issues appeared); from February 1907 headed the Datong School in Shaoxing, which Xu Xilin had opened as a front for revolutionary training, and organised the Restoration Army; refused to flee when warned, was captured on 13 July, refused to answer questions or write a confession under torture and was beheaded on 15 July 1907. Reference-work biography, admiring, built on earlier Chinese and Western biographies; notes that sources disagree on her birth year and several dates.

Lionel Giles, 'Ch'iu Chin: A Chinese Heroine', paper read to the China Society, London, 29 March 1917 (East and West, Ltd., 1917; Internet Archive scan, read in full as OCR text). Early English-language biography drawn from the account by Tao Chengzhang and from the recollections of her friend Xu Zihua; Giles also read the second number of her Chinese Women's Journal. Records her 1904 voyage to Japan, her return in protest in 1905-06, the failed bomb workshop in Shanghai, the journal, the Datong School, the plan for a rising on 19 July 1907, her refusal to leave, and her silence before the magistrate. Admiring, but he judges Xu Xilin's killing of the Anhui governor a tragic blunder and repeats Xu Zihua's remark that her unguarded cutting remarks helped lead to her death.

Hu Ying, 'Writing Qiu Jin's Life: Wu Zhiying and Her Family Learning', Late Imperial China vol. 25 no. 2 (December 2004), pp. 119-160 (Johns Hopkins University Press; Project MUSE PDF, read). COUNTER-VOICE: scholarly study of how her friends Wu Zhiying, Xu Zihua and the essayist Zhang Binglin wrote her life within months of her death; shows that later citations turned her reply to Wu Zhiying into an openly anti-Manchu declaration, that her friends shaped her as a knight-errant (xia) figure for political reasons, and that her image became heavily symbolic. Also records (from Wu Zhiying's memoir) that in 1904 she diverted money saved for her Japan tuition to help a political prisoner of the 1898 reform, that she kept a Japanese sword and performed a sword dance for Wu in 1906, and that her adoption of the knight-errant persona may be partly strategic.

Xu Zihua, 'Jianhu nuxia Qiu jun mubiao' (tomb inscription for the woman knight of Mirror Lake, Qiu Jin), written in 1908 by her friend and fellow poet (Chinese text on Wikisource, read). Contemporary friend's testimony: she was clever and resolute, ambitious, fond of swordsmen's tales, wine and sword dancing; held a leading role among Chinese students in Tokyo and spoke on the platform; saved her own expenses to help others study; returned with the student walk-out of 1905-06, taught at the Xunxi school, took a poor pupil to Shanghai to finish her education and ran the Chinese Women's Journal; headed the Datong School, was killed on 6 June (lunar) 1907 aged 33; Xu also says her sharpness made her feared and resented. Partisan memorial text written to clear her name; used for specific acts, not for its praise.

Huang Hongshou, 'Guangfujun zhi dunzuo' (the setback of the Restoration Army), Qing shi jishi benmo (Narratives of Qing history), juan 72, 1915 (Chinese text on Wikisource, read). Republican-era historical compilation, sympathetic to the revolution: records the Datong School under her headship, that the Shaoxing gentleman Hu Daonan, who was her enemy, denounced the school to Prefect Gui Fu, the troops' night raid in which two students were killed, that no real evidence of a conspiracy was found while she was tortured, that she would not admit anything and wrote only the seven characters 'autumn rain, autumn wind, sorrow kills a person', her execution the next morning and the later denunciation of her tomb. Compilation of earlier reports, not an eyewitness account.

James Carter, 'A revolutionary against empire and patriarchy: the execution of Qiu Jin', The China Project, 15 July 2020 (historian's column drawing on Hu Ying's 'Burying Autumn', Jonathan Spence and Eileen Cheng; read in full). Independent modern summary: her unbinding of her feet and move to Japan in 1904 with jewellery sold for the passage, her December 1905 speech to Chinese students in Tokyo, her return in 1906, the journal, bomb-making instruction, the Datong post, refusal to confess when interrogated, and a note that sources differ on her birth year and on the interval between interrogation and execution.

Chinese University of Hong Kong, Research Centre for Translation, Renditions author page 'Qiu Jin 1875?-1907' (short profile, read). Describes her as the best known woman martyr and revolutionist of the late Qing, who left her family to study in Japan in 1904, promoted women's education after returning and was executed in 1907 for her part in planning an armed uprising; her work is collected in the Qiu Jin ji. Short institutional profile, used only to confirm the outline.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_qingshi, src_qiujin_carter | 1904-1907 | reference biography, early biography, republican chronicle, historian's column] She left husband and children in 1904, sold her jewellery and crossed to Japan alone, took part in a bomb workshop that exploded (Giles), then headed a school used for armed training; when students and visitors urged her to flee in July 1907 she stayed, and the school was raided (Gale, Giles, Carter, Qing shi). The exposure was personal and also fell on her students, so impact is dual-edged. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 80 / 0.64 documented to 74 / 0.56 strong inference because the refusal to flee and the 1904 departure come from the Tao Chengzhang-derived biographies (Gale, Giles, and Carter retelling them), only the raid itself has an independent chronicle (Qing shi), the bomb accident is in Giles alone, and the martyr tradition is the kind Hu Ying shows was shaped after her death.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_qingshi, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_xuzihua | 1905-1907 | reference biography, republican chronicle, early biography, friend's inscription] She urged the 1905 student walk-out against the Japanese regulations, earned the enmity of a local gentleman by sharp remarks that Xu Zihua said made her feared and resented, and under torture would give no confession, writing only a line of poetry (Gale, Giles, Qing shi). The courage under interrogation is consistent across accounts; the earlier quarrels are described mainly by her friends. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.58 to 72 / 0.54 because her silence under torture is told within a martyr tradition, and the quarrel with the gentleman is reported only through her friend Xu Zihua.

social_assertiveness.rationale: [src_qiujin_xuzihua, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_carter | 1904-1907 | friend's inscription, early biography, reference biography, historian's column] Xu Zihua says she spoke on the platform at the large student meetings in Tokyo; Giles gives the substance of a public lecture on foot-binding from a popular Chinese account, and Gale records her lectures on revolution and gender equality and her organising of an oratory society; Carter adds a December 1905 speech in front of Lu Xun. She did this as a woman in male dress at a time when few women spoke in public, but the speech texts come from later popular accounts. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.58 to 72 / 0.54 because the wording of her speeches comes from later popular accounts and a friend's eulogy; the knife-on-the-table anecdote is not used.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_qiujin_xuzihua, src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles | 1904-1907 | friend's inscription, reference biography, early biography] Xu Zihua says her speeches moved hearers to tears, Giles says student audiences were rallied to her return-home league, and Gale says she reportedly won over soldiers in Hangzhou. The 'moved to tears' claim is from a friend's memorial text and the soldier claim is hedged in the source, so this is an inference from reported effect rather than documented persuading of named people. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.48 to 62 / 0.44 because the effect on audiences is reported in a memorial text and the soldier recruitment is hedged by the source.

leadership_drive.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_xuzihua, src_qiujin_qingshi | 1905-1907 | reference biography, early biography, friend's inscription, republican chronicle] Gale says she was named head of the Revolutionary Alliance's Zhejiang branch in 1905 and organised the Restoration Army; Xu Zihua says she led a society among the students in Japan; Giles and the Qing shi record her appointment as head of the Datong School, where she drilled students and recruited among soldiers. Headship is recorded by four accounts, though the Zhejiang branch claim is in Gale alone and the rising itself failed. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.6 to 70 / 0.54 because the Zhejiang branch headship and the Restoration Army rest on Gale alone and the Datong headship on accounts of the same tradition.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_xuzihua, src_qiujin_hu2004, src_qiujin_carter | 1904-1907 | reference biography, early biography, friend's inscription, scholarly study, historian's column] She initiated the move to Japan against her family's wishes, founded the Chinese Women's Journal in Shanghai with Xu Zihua's funds, joined a revolutionary society on her own introduction from Tao Chengzhang, took on the Datong School, and set up a branch of the society in Shanghai (Gale, Giles, Xu Zihua). Hu Ying shows she also acted unprompted for others (the 1904 gift to a political prisoner). Several independent initiatives across three years. Lead review lowered this row to 74 / 0.58 because the early biographies of a martyr figure are partly commemorative, so independence of the initiative accounts is limited.

autonomy_need.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_hu2004, src_qiujin_carter | 1896-1906 | reference biography, early biography, scholarly study, historian's column] She was married by arrangement in 1896, found the marriage uncongenial, and in 1904 left it, travelling alone to Japan with money from selling her jewellery; Gale and Carter add that she unbound her feet and dressed as a man, and Giles says the couple agreed to separate. Hu Ying warns that the male persona may be partly strategic, so the dress is not scored as evidence; the separation and independent travel are the basis.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_qiujin_hu2004, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_xuzihua, src_qiujin_gale | 1904-1907 | scholarly study, early biography, friend's inscription, reference biography] Her friend Wu Zhiying's memoir, discussed by Hu Ying and repeated by Giles, says she sent part of the money saved for her own studies to help a jailed 1898 reformer without giving her name; Xu Zihua says she saved her own expenses to help others study and took a poor pupil to Shanghai to finish her schooling; she founded a women's journal and headed a school. Two friends' testimonies describe concrete acts of sacrifice for others and a public cause. CONCENTRATION (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.58 documented to 70 / 0.52 strong inference because both acts of giving come from two close friends writing to defend her memory, and Giles repeats the first from Wu Zhiying rather than from an independent witness.

collaboration.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_xuzihua | 1905-1907 | reference biography, early biography, friend's inscription] She worked within a network: Tao Chengzhang's introduction, Xu Xilin and the Restoration Society, Xu Zihua's funding and school, a joint journal, and a plan co-ordinated with the Anhui and Jinhua groups (Gale, Giles). Giles also reports the plan was spoiled when others acted early, and Xu Zihua says her sharp remarks cost her allies, so the evidence is of network membership rather than smooth co-operation.

planning_orientation.rationale: [src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_gale | 1907 | early biography, reference biography] Giles, quoting a friend's account, says she made a secret survey of the roads around Hangzhou and drew a military map, and set a coordinated rising for 19 July, with a first attack to wait until the Hangzhou garrison had marched out; Gale says she imposed tight organisation on the Restoration Army. The plan was overtaken when others rose early and the Anhui assassination exposed the network, so the planning is documented in outline but its quality is not shown.

persistence.rationale: [src_qiujin_gale, src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_carter | 1905-1907 | reference biography, early biography, historian's column] After leaving the student movement in Tokyo she returned to China and kept organising: she toured Zhejiang to prepare a rising after the Jiangxi rising collapsed (Giles), kept publishing the journal as funds ran short (Gale: two issues only) and continued after the Anhui failure until arrested. Repeated recovery from set-backs is shown, though the journal and the rising both ended quickly.

adaptability.rationale: [src_qiujin_giles, src_qiujin_gale | 1905-1907 | early biography, reference biography] Giles says that after the bomb workshop accident she turned to a new outlet in the women's journal, and after leaving her Tokyo course in protest she returned to teach in a Zhejiang girls' school; Gale records the same return and teaching. She moved between teaching, publishing and conspiracy as circumstances changed, but there are few documented instances of changing her approach.

portrait.source: Photograph of Qiu Jin (photographer not named, taken before her death in 1907) printed as a full-page plate with the caption 秋瑾女士遺像 (Portrait of Ms. Qiu Jin) and the donor line 王燦芝女士贈刊 (contributed by Ms. Wang Canzhi, her daughter) in the Shanghai literary magazine Ren Jian Shi (The Human World, ed. Lin Yutang; Liangyou), issue 28, 1935. Page scan on Wikimedia Commons (file 秋瑾女士遺像.png, 1975 x 2880, uploaded 2023 from issue 28); the photograph was cropped from the page (caption and margins removed) and downscaled to 733 x 1000 with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: first published in China in 1935; under the 1990 PRC Copyright Law (arts. 21 and 55) the term for a photograph ran 50 years to the end of the 50th year after first publication (end of 1985), so it had expired before the law took effect in 1991 and was not protected in China on 1 January 1996; US copyright was therefore not restored. Photographer unknown; no holder statement found.
portrait.attribution: Photographer unknown; portrait of Qiu Jin contributed by her daughter Wang Canzhi, Ren Jian Shi (The Human World) no. 28, Shanghai, 1935 (page scan on Wikimedia Commons; cropped and downscaled).
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer (printed in Ren Jian Shi, Shanghai)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: RISKY (Stage B) / REPLACED after one bounded retry. The lead (Commons 'Qiu jin.jpg', Japanese-dress studio photograph, 550 x 785, unknown photographer, source a Chinese website, no holder record, no documented first publication) did not survive: with no documented publication before 1931 it cannot be shown to be public domain in the United States (an unpublished 1900-07 work would not be), and the Commons template alone was not relied on. Alternative routes tried: (1) Wisconsin Historical Society photograph of Qiu Jin in European dress (c. 1910, Catt collection, record IM111120) read: 'no copyright - United States' but written permission, no redistribution and no alteration beyond cropping: rejected; (2) 1919 Shanghai plate 'Qiu Jin nuxia yirong ji jiuyi tu' in Zhijia quanshu (Commons, published before 1931, PD) read: the portrait is only a small oval of about 135 x 210 px, too small to use without upscaling: kept as a rights-clear but low-resolution fallback; (3) Giles 1917 pamphlet (Internet Archive PDF) has no plate; (4) Library of Congress pictures search: no item; British Museum 'China's hidden century' portrait page returned 403 (bot wall, not bypassed). SHIPPED: the plate in Ren Jian Shi no. 28 (1935): printed caption 秋瑾女士遺像 and donor line 王燦芝女士贈刊 (Wang Canzhi is named as her daughter in Gale and on the Commons category), photographer unknown. RIGHTS: first published in Shanghai in 1935; 1990 PRC Copyright Law art. 21 (photographs 50 years from first publication) and art. 55 (works already out of term at 1 June 1991 not protected) read on Wikisource; so PD in the PRC before the 1996 URAA date and not restored in the US; Commons template PD-China-1996 read and consistent. CAVEATS: no authoritative holder or item record exists (Commons does not name a library; the scan provenance and exact issue date are unknown, the issue number and year are from the Commons file page, and the magazine's run of 42 semi-monthly issues in 1934-35 is consistent with 1935); the photograph's own date and photographer are unknown; the Commons upload was fetched through thumb.php at its native width (1975 px) because upload.wikimedia.org returned 429 for this shared network address, so the file is a re-rendered copy, not byte-identical to the original; kind likeness is based on the caption and the daughter's contribution, not on a lifetime print. PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-23, Wikidata API) Q465324 label 'Qiu Jin', description 'Chinese revolutionary, feminist, and writer (1875-1907)', ko label 추근, human, born 1875-11-08 (a second value 1879 also stored), died July 1907, citizenship Qing dynasty. REGION east_asia (Chinese precedent). ERA 20th_century (her activity runs 1904-1907). Nationality CN. ZERO POLITICS in scoring: she was an anti-Qing revolutionary, and the rows score only behaviour (travel, organising, speeches, refusing to flee, silence under torture), never the political cause or its justification. KOREAN NAME: 추근 (Korean Wikipedia title and Wikidata ko label), class authoritative-label; no other Korean source seen. ATTRIBUTION: limited_but_usable (a real, well-attested life, but the accounts after 1907 are shaped by a martyr tradition: Hu Ying shows later retellings changed her words and image). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Gernant, Qiu Jin, Women in World History (Gale). READ (7 sources besides Wikidata): Gale entry (full); Giles 1917 (full); Hu Ying 2004 (first 20 pages carefully, rest searched); Xu Zihua's 1908 tomb inscription (full); Qing shi jishi benmo juan 72 (full chapter section on Qiu Jin); Carter 2020; CUHK profile. NOT OPENED: Rankin 1975 and 1971, Hu Ying's Burying Autumn, Spence, Cheng, Hummel (lending-library only), Tao Chengzhang's own biography, her collected works. INDEPENDENT BEHAVIOURAL FAMILIES: three (the Tao Chengzhang-derived biographies, friends' testimony, the Republican chronicle) plus the scholarly counter-voice; Carter and CUHK are derivative. CONTRADICTIONS: birth year (1875/1877/1878/1879), execution-day details, the Datong date for the rising (6 or 19 July), whether she joined the Revolutionary Alliance in Tokyo or the Restoration Society first; none carded. Not scored: dress and persona (Hu Ying notes it may be strategic), the knife-on-the-table speech anecdote, bomb-making beyond one accident reported by Giles, her marriage as a private matter. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: PASS (Datong School, rising and execution; women's journal and advocacy; poetry). SELF-CALIBRATION: concentration lowered risk_tolerance (80/0.64 documented to 74/0.56 strong inference), leadership_drive (76/0.6 to 70/0.54), impact_motivation (76/0.58 documented to 70/0.52 strong inference); self-calibration lowered social_assertiveness (76/0.58 to 72/0.54), conflict_tolerance (76/0.58 to 72/0.54), persuasiveness (66/0.48 to 62/0.44); no row raised.
